title: Mitsitsin Iri: Labarin Wangari Maathai
title_en: A Tiny Seed: The Story of Wangari Maathai
author: Nicola Rijsdijk

pages.text: Sunan wannan yarinya Wangari Maathai, ‘yar kasar Kenya ce a gabashin Afrika.
pages.en: In a village on the slopes of Mount Kenya in East Africa, a little girl worked in the fields with her mother. Her name was Wangari.

pages.text: Ta na sha’awar zama a waje, shi ya sa ta shuka iri a lambun gidansu.
pages.en: Wangari loved being outside. In her family’s food garden she broke up the soil with her machete. She pressed tiny seeds into the warm earth.

pages.text: Lokacin da tafi san tafiya gida shi ne bayan faduwar rana, ta na bin kwararo dan zuwa gida ta na kuma kallan shuke-shuke.
pages.en:
Her favourite time of day was just after sunset. When it got too dark to see the plants, Wangari knew it was time to go home.

She would follow the narrow paths through the fields, crossing rivers as she went.

pages.text: Duk da kwazan da ta ke da shi, iyayanta ba sa san ta je makaranta domin taimaka masu aiki a gida. Da ta cika shekara bakwai sai yayanta ya rinjayi iyayenta domin ta je makaranta.
pages.en:
Wangari was a clever child and couldn’t wait to go to school. But her mother and father wanted her to stay and help them at home.

When she was seven years old, her big brother persuaded her parents to let her go to school.

pages.text: Wangari ta yi murna matuka lokacin da aka gaiya ce ta zuwa Amurka ta yi karatu, sakamakon kwazanta na san karatun littattafai.
pages.en:
She liked to learn! Wangari learnt more and more with every book she read. She did so well at school that she was invited to study in the United States of America.

Wangari was excited! She wanted to know more about the world.

pages.text: A Jami’ar Amuruka ta koyi sababin abubuwa da yawa, wadanda suka hada da rayuwar tsirai da yadda suke girma da yadda suke wasa da ‘yan uwanta a karkashin inuwar kyakkyawan bishiyoyin Kenya a daji.
pages.en: At the American university Wangari learnt many new things. She studied plants and how they grow. And she remembered how she grew: playing games with her brothers in the shade of the trees in the beautiful Kenyan forests.

pages.text: Da zarar ta koyi wani abu ya kan kara mata kaunar mutan Kenya, ta na son ganin su cikin farin ciki da ‘yanci, ta kan kuma tuna Afurika a matsayin gida.
pages.en:
The more she learnt, the more she realised that she loved the people of Kenya. She wanted them to be happy and free.

The more she learnt, the more she remembered her African home.

pages.text: Yayin da kamala karatun ta, sai ta dawo gida. Amma kasarta ta canja, manyan gonaki sun hade hade da hanya. Mata basu da itacen girki sanan jama’ar gari sun talauce, yara suna fama da yunwa.
pages.en: When she had finished her studies, she returned to Kenya. But her country had changed. Huge farms stretched across the land. Women had no wood to make cooking fires. The people were poor and the children were hungry.

pages.text: Wangari ta taimakawa mata sosai sun sami kudi saboda ta koya musu yadda za su shuka bishiyoyi su sayar dan taimakawa iyalensu. Wannan yasa mata suka zama masu alfahari da kansu.
pages.en: Wangari knew what to do. She taught the women how to plant trees from seeds. The women sold the trees and used the money to look after their families. The women were very happy. Wangari had helped them to feel powerful and strong.

pages.text: Bayan lokaci mai tsawo bishiyoyi sun girma sun zama daji, koguna suka fara gudanya, sakonta sai ya fara mamaye Afurika. A yau milliyoyin bishiyoyi sun samu a sakamakon gudunmuwar irin da Wangari ta samar.
pages.en: As time passed, the new trees grew into forests, and the rivers started flowing again. Wangari’s message spread across Africa. Today, millions of trees have grown from Wangari’s seeds.

pages.text: Mutanen duniya baki daya sun yaba da kwazon ta, saboda haka ne ma aka karama ta da shahararriyar kyautar nan ta zaman lafiya ta duniya (NOVEL). Ita ce mace ta farko da ta fara samun kyautar a Afurika.
pages.en: Wangari had worked hard. People all over the world took notice, and gave her a famous prize. It is called the Nobel Peace Prize, and she was the first African woman ever to receive it.

pages.text: Wangari ta mutu a shekara ta dubu biyu da sha daya (2011), amma mu kan tuna ta duk lokacin da muka ga kyawawan bishiyoyi.
pages.en: Wangari died in 2011, but we can think of her every time we see a beautiful tree.

title: Èso kékeré kan: Ìtàn tí Wangari Maathai
title_en: A Tiny Seed: The Story of Wangari Maathai
author: Nicola Rijsdijk

pages.text:
Ní abúlé kan lórí Òkè Kenya ní Ìlà-oòrùn Afrika, ọmọ kékeré kan ṣiṣẹ́ nínú oko pẹ̀lú
màmá rẹ̀. Orúkọ rẹ̀ ni Wangari.
pages.en: In a village on the slopes of Mount Kenya in East Africa, a little girl worked in the fields with her mother. Her name was Wangari.

pages.text:
Wangari fẹ́ràn láti wà ní ìta. Ní ọgbà ilé oúnjẹ ẹbí rẹ̀, ó tu ilẹ̀ pẹ̀lú àdá rẹ̀. Ó fi
àwọn èso kékeré sínú ilẹ̀.
pages.en: Wangari loved being outside. In her family’s food garden she broke up the soil with her machete. She pressed tiny seeds into the warm earth.

pages.text:
Àkókò tí ó fẹ́ràn ni ìrọ̀lẹ́. Nígbà tí alẹ́ bá ti lẹ́ jù, Wangari mọ̀ pé àkókò ti tó láti lọlé.
Ó máa gba ọ̀nà tínínrín inú oko tí ó wà ní ẹ̀gbẹ́ odò tí ó bá tí ń padà lọlé.
pages.en:
Her favourite time of day was just after sunset. When it got too dark to see the plants, Wangari knew it was time to go home.

She would follow the narrow paths through the fields, crossing rivers as she went.

pages.text:
Wangari jẹ́ ọlọ́gbọ́n ọmọ, kò lè dúró títí tí ó máa fi lọ sí ilé-ìwé. Ṣùgbọ́n màmá àti
bàbá rẹ̀ fẹ́ jẹ́kí ó dúró sílé láti ràn wọ́n lọ́wọ́. Nígbà tí ó jẹ́ ọmọ ọ̀dún méje, ẹ̀gbọ́n
rẹ̀ ọkùnrin sọ fún àwọn òbí wọn kí wọ́n jẹ́ kí ó lọ sí ilé-ìwé.
pages.en:
Wangari was a clever child and couldn’t wait to go to school. But her mother and father wanted her to stay and help them at home.

When she was seven years old, her big brother persuaded her parents to let her go to school.

pages.text:
Ó fẹ́ràn láti kàwé!
Wangari kọ́ oríṣiríṣi nǹkan nínú ìwé tí ó kà.
Ó ṣe dáradára ní ilé-ìwé débi pé wọ́n pè wá sí ìlú Amerika láti kàwé.
Inú Wangari dùn gán an ni! Ó fẹ́ mọ̀ si nípa gbogbo ayé.
pages.en:
She liked to learn! Wangari learnt more and more with every book she read. She did so well at school that she was invited to study in the United States of America.

Wangari was excited! She wanted to know more about the world.

pages.text:
Ní Yunifásítì kan ní ìlú Amerika, Wangari kọ́ ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ nǹkan tuntun. Ó kọ́ nípa bí
àwọn ewé ṣe ń dàgbà. Ó rántí bí òun ṣe dàgbà: bí òun ṣe ń ṣeré pẹ̀lú àwọn ẹbí rẹ̀
lábẹ́ àwọn igi inú igbó Kenya.
pages.en: At the American university Wangari learnt many new things. She studied plants and how they grow. And she remembered how she grew: playing games with her brothers in the shade of the trees in the beautiful Kenyan forests.

pages.text:
Bí ó ṣe ń kàwé si ni ó ń ri bí òun ṣe fẹ́ràn àwọn ènìyàn Kenya. Ó fẹ́ jẹ́ kí wọ́n ní
ayọ̀ àtí òmìnira. Bí ó ṣe ń kàwé si ni ó ń rántí ilé rẹ̀ ní Afrika.
pages.en:
The more she learnt, the more she realised that she loved the people of Kenya. She wanted them to be happy and free.

The more she learnt, the more she remembered her African home.

pages.text:
Nígbá tí ó parí ẹ̀kọ́ rẹ̀, ó padà sí Kenya.
Ṣùgbọ́n orílẹ̀-èdè rẹ̀ ti yípadà. Àwọn oko ńlá ti pọ̀si nílẹ̀.
Àwọn obìnrin kò ní igi láti fi dáná.
Àwọn ènìyàn tòṣì. Ebi sì ń pa àwọn ọmọdé.
pages.en: When she had finished her studies, she returned to Kenya. But her country had changed. Huge farms stretched across the land. Women had no wood to make cooking fires. The people were poor and the children were hungry.

pages.text:
Wangari mọ nǹkan tí óun lè ṣe. Ó kọ́ àwọn obìnrin láti gbin igi pẹ̀lú èso.
Àwọn obìnrin náà ta àwọn igi náà,wọ́n sì lo owó tí wọ́n rí láti fi tọ́jú ẹbí wọn.
Inú àwọn obìnrin náà dùn púpọ̀. Wangari ràn wọ́n lọ́wọ́ láti lè borí wàhálà wọn.
pages.en: Wangari knew what to do. She taught the women how to plant trees from seeds. The women sold the trees and used the money to look after their families. The women were very happy. Wangari had helped them to feel powerful and strong.

pages.text:
Lẹ́hìn àkókò púpọ̀, àwọn igi tuntun náà dàgbà sí igbó, àwọn odò náà sì padà.
Gbogbo ènìyàn ní Afrika ni ó gbọ́ nǹkan tí Wangari ṣe.
Lónìí, ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ àwọn igi ni ó ti dàgbà nípasẹ èso ti Wangari.
pages.en: As time passed, the new trees grew into forests, and the rivers started flowing again. Wangari’s message spread across Africa. Today, millions of trees have grown from Wangari’s seeds.

pages.text:
Wangari tí ṣiṣẹ́ gan an. Gbogbo
ènìyàn káàkiri àgbáyé ni ó mọ̀,
wọ́n sì fun ní ẹ̀bùn ńlá kan. Wọ́n
ń pè é ní ẹ̀bùn ti Nobel Peace,
òun sì ni obìnrin àkọ́kọ́ tí ó kọ́kọ́
gbà á.
pages.en: Wangari had worked hard. People all over the world took notice, and gave her a famous prize. It is called the Nobel Peace Prize, and she was the first African woman ever to receive it.

pages.text:
Wangari kú ní ọ̀dún 2011, ṣùgbọ́n a lè ronú nípa rẹ̀ nígbàkígbà tí a bá rí igi arẹwà
kan.
pages.en: Wangari died in 2011, but we can think of her every time we see a beautiful tree.

pages.text: Adìyẹ àti Ọ̀ọ̀kùn jẹ́ ọ̀rẹ́.
pages.en: Chicken and Millipede were friends. But they were always competing with each other. One day they decided to play football to see who the best player was.

pages.text: Wọ́n lọ gbá bọ́ọ̀lù.
pages.en: They went to the football field and started their game. Chicken was fast, but Millipede was faster. Chicken kicked far, but Millipede kicked further. Chicken started to feel grumpy.

pages.text: Adìyẹ ní ó múlé.
pages.en: They decided to play a penalty shoot-out. First Millipede was goal keeper. Chicken scored only one goal. Then it was the chicken’s turn to defend the goal.

pages.text: Ọ̀ọ̀kùn gbá bọ́ọ̀lù wọlé.
pages.en:
Millipede kicked the ball and scored.

Millipede dribbled the ball and scored. Millipede headed the ball and scored. Millipede scored five goals.

pages.text: Inú bí Adìyẹ.
pages.en: Chicken was furious that she lost. She was a very bad loser. Millipede started laughing because his friend was making such a fuss.

pages.text: Adìyẹ ṣá Ọ̀ọ̀kùn jẹ, ó gbée mì.
pages.en: Chicken was so angry that she opened her beak wide and swallowed the millipede.

pages.text: Adìyẹ padé ìyá Ọ̀ọ̀kùn.
pages.en:
As Chicken was walking home, she met Mother Millipede. Mother Millipede asked, “Have you seen my child?” Chicken didn’t say anything.

Mother Millipede was worried.

pages.text: “Ìyá mi, ẹ gbà mi1” Ọ̀ọ̀kùn paríwo.
pages.en: Then Mother Millipede heard a tiny voice. “Help me mom!” cried the voice. Mother Millipede looked around and listened carefully. The voice came from inside the chicken.

pages.text: Ara Adìyẹ kò yá.
pages.en: Mother Millipede shouted, “Use your special power my child!” Millipedes can make a bad smell and a terrible taste. Chicken began to feel ill.

pages.text: Ọ̀ọ̀kùn kò dára rára lẹ́nu rẹ́.
pages.en: Chicken burped. Then she swallowed and spat. Then she sneezed and coughed. And coughed. The millipede was disgusting!

pages.text: Adìyẹ bi Ọ̀ọ̀kùn jádé láti ikùn rẹ̀.Ọ̀ọ̀kùn sáré, ó sálọ.
pages.en: Chicken coughed until she coughed out the millipede that was in her stomach. Mother Millipede and her child crawled up a tree to hide.

pages.text: Adìyẹ àti Ọ̀ọ̀kùn dí ọ̀tá.
pages.en: From that time, chickens and millipedes were enemies.

time crossing the road
because she knows she
paid her fare in full.

pages.text: Before before, three girls go pack wood.
pages.en:
A long time ago, three girls went
out to collect wood.

pages.text: Weda hot no be small, so dem come go river go swim. Dem play and swim inside water.
pages.en:
It was a hot day so they went down
to the river to swim.
They played and splashed and
swam in the water.

pages.text: At ones dem come see say time don go. Dem come rush go back village.
pages.en:
Suddenly, they realised that it was
late.
They hurried back to the village.

pages.text: Wen dem don near house, Nozibele touch em neck. E come know say e don leave em chain! E beg em friends to follow am go back but dem say time don too go far.
pages.en:
When they were nearly home,
Nozibele put her hand to her neck.
She had forgotten her necklace!
“Please come back with me!” she
begged her friends.
But her friends said it was too late.

pages.text: Na so Nozibele come go back by emsef. E see the chain na em e tuke go house. Na so e come miss road.
pages.en:
So Nozibele went back to the river
alone.
She found her necklace and hurried
home.
But she got lost in the dark.

pages.text: E come see light dey shine for one house far far. Na so e rush go there go knock d door.
pages.en:
In the distance she saw light
coming from a hut.
She hurried towards it and knocked
at the door.

pages.text: Shoo, na dog open door o. D dog say, “wetin you want?” “ Nozibele come say e miss road, i dey look for were to sleep,” ”come inside, or I go bite u oo! D dog tell am. Na so Nozibele enter o.
pages.en:
To her surprise, a dog opened the
door and said, “What do you want?”
“I’m lost and I need a place to
sleep,” said Nozibele.
“Come in, or I’ll bite you!” said the
dog.
So Nozibele went in.

pages.text: Dog come say, “oya cook for me” e come ansa am say e never cook for dog before o. Dog come say, “cook, or I go bite you oo!” na so Nozibele come cook food for dog.
pages.en:
Then the dog said, “Cook for me!”
“But I’ve never cooked for a dog
before,” she answered.
“Cook, or I’ll bite you!” said the dog.
So Nozibele cooked some food for
the dog.

pages.text: Dog come say, “do my bed!” e ansa am say e never do bed for dog before oo. Dog come say, “do my bed or I go bite you!” na so Nozibele come do bed for dog.
pages.en:
Then the dog said, “Make the bed
for me!”
Nozibele answered, “I’ve never
made a bed for a dog.”
“Make the bed, or I’ll bite you!” the
dog said.
So Nozibele made the bed.

pages.text: Na so dog come put Nozibele for work. day by day e go cook, sweep, wash for dog. Dog come tell am one day say, “Nozibele, i wan go see my friend dem. Make you sweep d house, cook and wash cloth before i return.
pages.en:
Every day she had to cook and
sweep and wash for the dog.
Then one day the dog said,
“Nozibele, today I have to visit
some friends. Sweep the house,
cook the food and wash my things
before I come back.”

pages.text: As dog comot, na so Nozibele comot three of her from head. E keep one under bed, another one for back of door then one for d kraal. e come skele go house with speed.
pages.en:
As soon as the dog had gone,
Nozibele took three hairs from her
head.
She put one hair under the bed, one
behind the door, and one in the
kraal.
Then she ran home as fast as she
could.

pages.text: As Dog return, e come look e no see Nozibele. Na so e come shout “Nozibele, were u dey na?” “I dey unda d bed,” d first hair ansa. “I dey back of door,” d second hair ansa. “I dey inside kraal,” d third hair ansa.
pages.en:
When the dog came back, he looked
for Nozibele.
“Nozibele, where are you?” he
shouted.
“I’m here, under the bed,” said the
first hair.
“I’m here, behind the door,” said the
second hair.
“I’m here, in the kraal,” said the
third hair.

pages.text: Na now d Dog come get the gist say Nozibele don do am wayo. Na so Dog come para run go reach d village. Nozibele bros dem don set dey wait am with heavy stick. Na so Dog do reverse tuke wen no one see am since.
pages.en:
Then the dog knew that Nozibele
had tricked him.
So he ran and ran all the way to the
village.
But Nozibele’s brothers were
waiting there with big sticks.
The dog turned and ran away and
has never been seen since.

pages.text: Na Khalai be dis. She be seven years. D meaning of her name na ‘good one’ for dem dialect, wen be Lubukusu.
pages.en:
This is Khalai.
She is seven years old.
Her name means ‘the
good one’ in her
language, Lubukusu.

pages.text: Khalai wake up begin yan with orange tree. “Abeg orange tree, dey grow oo make we for dey lick plenty orange wen ripe.”
pages.en:
Khalai wakes up and
talks to the orange tree.
“Please orange tree,
grow big and give us
lots of ripe oranges.”

pages.text: Khalai dey tricke go school. For road na so she go dey yan with grass. “Abeg oo grass, grow make u dey fresh and make u no die oo.”
pages.en:
Khalai walks to school.
On the way she talks to
the grass. “Please
grass, grow greener
and don’t dry up.”

pages.text: Khalai waka pass bush flower. “Abeg oo flower, make u grow fine fine oo make I for dey put you for hair.”
pages.en:
Khalai passes wild
flowers. “Please
flowers, keep blooming
so I can put you in my
hair.”

pages.text: For school, Khalai go talk to tree wen dey center of compound. “Abeg oo tree, make ur branches dey spreed oo make we for fit dey siddon read under your shade oo.”
pages.en:
At school, Khalai talks
to the tree in the
middle of the
compound. “Please
tree, put out big
branches so we can
read under your shade.”

pages.text: Khalai dey yan to flower wen surround her school. “Abeg oo flower, make grow strong oo so yeye person no go fit enter our school.”
pages.en:
Khalai talks to the
hedge around her school.
“Please grow strong
and stop bad people
from coming in.”

pages.text: Wen Khalai come back for school, she go look d orange tree come ask am, Your orange dem never ripe?”
pages.en:
When Khalai returns
home from school, she
visits the orange tree.
“Are your oranges ripe
yet?” asks Khalai.

pages.text: “D orange dem still never ripe oo” hmmmn. “I go see you tomorrow oo orange tree,” “maybe tomorrow go beta and I fit get ripe orange for mysef!”
pages.en:
“The oranges are still
green,” sighs Khalai.
“I will see you tomorrow
orange tree,” says
Khalai. “Perhaps then
you will have a ripe
orange for me!”

pages.text: My small brother sabi sleep well well. I dey quick get up as bigger boy!
pages.en: My little brother sleeps very late. I wake early, because I am great!

pages.text: Na me dey let sun enter inside.
pages.en: I am the one who lets in the sun.

pages.text: You be my shine shine bobo mama go say.
pages.en: “You’re my morning star,” says Ma.

pages.text: I sabi bath mysef nobody dey help me.
pages.en: I wash myself, I don’t need any help.

pages.text: I no dey fear cold water and blue soap wen dey smell
pages.en: I can cope with cold water and blue smelly soap.

pages.text: Mama go say no forget your teeth o! I go tell am say no shaking.
pages.en: Ma reminds, “Don’t forget teeth.” I reply, “Never, not me!”

pages.text: Wen I don bath finish, I go salute grandpapa and aunty, and tell dem say make today beta oo.
pages.en: After washing, I greet Grandpa and Auntie, and wish them a good day.

pages.text: Den I go wear my cloth by myself, “I tell mama say I be bigger boy.
pages.en: Then I dress myself, “I’m big now Ma,” I say.

pages.text: I fit do my buttons and tie my shoe.
pages.en: I can close my buttons and buckle my shoes.

pages.text: I dey tell my small brother all the gist from school.
pages.en: And I make sure little brother knows all the school news.

pages.text: For school, I dey try as my power gree me
pages.en: In class I do my best in every way.

pages.text: I dey do plenty things everyday. But na play I like pass.
pages.en: I do all these good things every day. But the thing I like most, is to play and play!

pages.text: Tingi de stay with grandma.
pages.en: Tingi lived with his grandmother.

pages.text: E dey take care of d cow with her.
pages.en: He used to look after the cows with her.

pages.text: One day soldiers come.
pages.en: One day the soldiers came.

pages.text: Dem come carry the cows go.
pages.en: They took the cows away.

pages.text: Tingi and em grandma run come hide.
pages.en: Tingi and his grandmother ran away and hid.

pages.text: Dem hide for bush till night come.
pages.en: They hid in the bush until night.

pages.text: The soldiers den come back.
pages.en: Then the soldiers came back.

pages.text: Grandma come hide Tingi under leaves.
pages.en: Grandmother hid Tingi under the leaves.

pages.text: One soldiers carry leg on top am, e no shake at all.
pages.en: One of the soldiers put his foot right on him, but he kept quiet.

pages.text: Wen dem don go, Tingi and em grandma come out.
pages.en: When it was safe, Tingi and his grandmother came out.

pages.text: Dem creep go house small small.
pages.en: They crept home very quietly.

title: Count animals
author: Zanele Buthelezi, Thembani Dladla, Clare Verbeek

pages.text: One elephant dey go drink water.
pages.en: One elephant is going to drink water.

pages.text: Two giraffes dey go drink water.
pages.en: Two giraffes are going to drink water.

pages.text: Three buffaloes and four birds sef dey go drink water.
pages.en: Three buffaloes and four birds are also going to drink water.

pages.text: Five Impales and six pigs dey waka go d water.
pages.en: Five impalas and six warthogs are walking to the water.

pages.text: Seven Zibras dey run go the water.
pages.en: Seven zebras are running to the water.

pages.text: Eight frogs and nine fish dey swim inside d water.
pages.en: Eight frogs and nine fish are swimming in the water.

pages.text: One lion shout. Em sef wan drink water. Na who dey fear lion?
pages.en: One lion roars. He also wants to drink. Who is afraid of the lion?

pages.text: One elephant dey drink water with lion.
pages.en: One elephant is drinking water with the lion.

pages.text: Yana son abinci, amma lalaci kan hana shi dafawa. Annasi ya je gidan Zomo ya ce in zo muci kayan lambu?
pages.en:
Once upon a time, there was a
spider called Anansi.
He was too lazy to cook his own
food. Instead, he used to visit his
friends and eat the delicious food
they had cooked.

pages.text: Zomo ya ce, “e”, amma ka taya ni juya miyar”. Anansi ya ce “bari in dawo”.
pages.en:
One day, he was walking past
Rabbit's house when he smelled
something cooking.
"Greens!" he said excitedly.
"They're not quite ready yet," said
Rabbit. "You can help me with the
washing up in the mean time."
"Sorry, I have things to do. I'll come
back later," said Anansi.

pages.text: Anansi ya saka yana a kafarsa a jikin tukunyar Zomo. “Ka ja yanar idan kayan lambun sun nuna”, in ji Anansi.
pages.en:
"How will I call you when they're
ready?" asked Rabbit.
Anansi thought for a minute.
"I'll spin a web," he said, "and tie
one end around my leg and one end
to your pot. When the greens are
ready, pull on the web string and I'll
come right away."
So Anansi tied the web to the pot,
and walked on.

pages.text: “Birrai, in zo mu ci wakenku?” “E. In ka taya mu sara”. “Zan dawo,” inji Anansi. Ya kuma saka yana.
pages.en:
A short while later he saw Monkey
and his wife, cooking some beans in
a large pot.
"Come and join us!" they said. "The
beans are nearly ready."
"Sorry, I have things to do," said
Anansi before they could ask him to
help.
"But let me tie one end of this web
around my leg and one end to your
pot. When the beans are ready, pull
on the web string, and I'll come."

pages.text: “Aladen dawa, in zo muci dankalinka?” E. Tai ma keni in. “Zan dawo,” inji Anansi. Ya kuma saka yana.
pages.en:
He walked on until he smelled
sweet potatoes.
"Anansi," called his friend Warthog.
"My pot is full of sweet potatoes
and honey! Come and share my
food with me. Here's a fork for you
to help me stir."
"I'll come back later," said Anansi
quickly. "But let me tie one end of
this web around my leg and one
end to your pot. When the sweet
potatoes are ready, pull on the web
string, and I'll come."

pages.text: “Aladen dawa, in zo muci dankalinka?” E. Tai ma keni in. “Zan dawo,” inji Anansi. Ya kuma saka yana.
pages.en:
By the time Anansi arrived at the
river, each of his eight legs was tied
to a different pot of delicious food.
Just then, Anansi felt a tug on one
of his legs.
"Rabbit's food is ready!" he said,
licking his lips.

pages.text: Duka kwafafuwan takwas a ka dinga jan su! “Ku bar ja!” Anansi ya ji ja a kafa ta biyu. Sannan ta uku.
pages.en:
He felt a second tug.
And a third.
And a fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh,
eighth...
Everyone was pulling on the web
strings at the same time!
"Stop! Stop!" he cried in pain, as
his legs were stretched thinner and
thinner.
But no one could hear him.

pages.text: Duka kwafafuwan takwas a ka dinga jan su! “Ku bar ja!”
pages.en:
Finally, the web strings could hold
no longer. They snapped one by
one.
Anansi rolled into the river to
soothe his painful legs. But his legs
would not return to their normal
shape.
And he was too embarrassed to go
to any of his friends and share their
food that day.

pages.text:
Ní ọjọ́ kan, Anansi aláǹtakùn mú àwọn iṣu láti ọgbà-oko rẹ̀.Àwọn iṣu aládùn kù, nítorí náà ó dín wọn dáradára lórí iná.

Lẹ́hìn náà, ó jòkó láti jẹ wọ́n.
pages.en:
One day, Anansi the spider picked
some yams from his garden.
They were extra beautiful delicious
yams, so he baked them carefully in
the fire.
Then he sat down to eat them up.

pages.text:
Bí Anansi ṣe fẹ́ jẹ́ iṣu àkọ́kọ́, ó gbọ́ pé ẹnikan kan ilẹ̀kùn rẹ́. “Rárá o!”

Anasi ronú. “Ta ni ó lè jẹ́?” Ṣùgbọ́n ó ṣí ilẹ̀kùn rẹ̀.

Níbẹ̀ ni Ìjàpá, ó rí bí i ẹni tí ó rẹ̀ púpọ̀. Ìjàpá ní, “Anansi, jọ̀wọ́ jẹ́ kín wọlé. Mo ti rín jìnà lónìí, ó tí rẹ̀mi àti wípé ebi ń pámi.”

Nítorí náà kí ni Anansi le ṣe ju kí ó jẹ́kí ó wọ́lé.
pages.en:
Just as Anansi was about to put the
first bite in his mouth, he heard a
knock on his door. "Oh, no!"
thought Anansi. "Who can that be?"
But he opened the door.
There was Turtle, who looked very
tired. Turtle said, "Anansi, please let
me in. I've walked so far today, and
I'm so tired and hungry."
So what could Anansi do but let him
in?

pages.text:
Anansi ní ahun gan an ni débi pé kò lè fún ẹnikẹ́ni jẹ lára iṣu aládùn rẹ̀. Nítorí náà, ó ṣe ìpinu kan.

Ní Ìjàpá ṣe jòkó sí orí tábìlì tí ó fẹ́ fọwọ́ kan àwọn iṣu rẹ̀. Anansi pariwo mọ́, “Ìjàpá, ọwọ́ rẹ̀ ti dọ̀tí jù! O kòlè jẹun pẹ̀lú dídọ̀tí yìí! Lọ fọ ọwọ́ rẹ̀."Ọwọ́ Ìjàpá dọ̀tí ní tòótọ́. Nítorí náà, ó wọ́ lọ sí odò, fọ ọwọ́ rẹ̀, ó sì wọ́ padà.
pages.en:
Anansi was too selfish to share his
beautiful delicious yams with
anybody else. So he came up with a
nasty plan.
Just as Turtle sat down at the table
and began to reach for some yams,
Anansi yelled at him, "Turtle, your
hands are all dirty! You can't eat
with your hands all dirty! Go wash
them."
Turtle's hands really were dirty. So
he slowly crawled to the river,
washed his hands, and then crawled
back.

pages.text: Ṣùgbọ́n Anansi ti bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ní kó gbogbo àwọn iṣu náà jẹ. Nígbà tí Ìjàpá fi padà, ó ri pé gbogbo àwọn iṣu náà ti lọ.Ìjàpá wo Anansi. “Ó ṣé tí o pè wá fún oúnjẹ alẹ́. Tí o bá wá sí ilé mi, jọ̀wọ́ wọ́lé kín lè san ore yìí padà fún ẹ,” Ìjàpá dáhùn.Ìjàpá sì bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ní wọ́ lọ sí ilé rẹ̀.
pages.en:
But meanwhile Anansi had started
gobbling up the yams. By the time
Turtle got back, he saw that the
yams were all gone.
Turtle looked at Anansi. "Thank you
for inviting me to dinner. If you're
ever near my house, please come
by and let me return the favour,"
said Turtle.
And Turtle began crawling slowly
away to his house.

pages.text:
Lẹ́hìn ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ àkókò, Anansi bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ronú bí Ìjàpá ṣe pinu láti fún ní oúnjẹ alẹ́. Nítorí náà, ní ọjọ́ kan, ó lọ sí ilé Ìjàpá.

Anansi dé ilé Ìjàpá ní àkókò oúnjẹ́ alẹ́, bí oòrùn ṣe ń múra láti wọ̀. Ìjàpá sùn sí orí àpáta, ó ń ṣeré, bí àwọn Ìjàpá ṣe máa ń ṣe.

Nígbà tí Ìjàpá rí Anansi, ó ní, “Báwo ni, Anansi, ṣé o wá láti jẹ oúnjẹ alẹ́ pẹ̀lú mi ni?”

Anansi sì sọpé, “Bẹ́ẹ̀ni, èyí dára púpọ̀, o ṣé.” Ebi sì bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí i páa.
pages.en:
As time went by, Anansi began to
think more and more about how
Turtle had promised to feed him a
free dinner. So one day he walked
over to Turtle's house.
Anansi got to Turtle's house just
about dinnertime, as the sun was
going down over the river. Turtle
was lying on a rock in the sun,
warming himself up, as turtles do.
When Turtle saw Anansi, he said,
"Hello there, Anansi, have you
come to have dinner with me?"
And Anansi said, "Yes, that would
be very nice, thank you." He was
getting hungrier and hungrier.

pages.text:
Nítorí náà, Ìjàpá wọ inú odò lọ sí ìsàlẹ̀ láti lọ ṣètò ṣílẹ̀ fún oúnjẹ́ alẹ́ náà. Anansi dúró ní orí àpáta lẹ́bàá odò.

Láìpẹ́ Ìjàpá wẹ̀ wá sí òkè orí omi, o ní “Óyá Anansi, gbogbo nǹkan ti wà nílẹ̀, jọ̀wọ́ jẹ́ kí a jọ̀ jẹun." Ìjàpá wẹ̀ padà lọ sí ìsàlẹ̀ láti lọ bẹ́rẹ́ sí ní jẹ àwọn ewé tí ó ṣètò fún oúnjẹ.
pages.en:
So Turtle dived down to the bottom
of the river to set the table for
dinner and get everything ready.
Anansi waited on the rocks by the
shore.
Soon Turtle swam back up and said,
"Oh Anansi, it is all ready now,
please join me for dinner." And
Turtle dived down again and began
to eat the green leaves he had for
dinner.

pages.text: Anansi gbìyànjú láti wọ inú odò lọ sí ìsàlẹ̀, ṣùgbọ́n aláńtakùn ni kì í ṣe Ìjàpá, kò lè wẹ̀ sísàlẹ̀. Ó kan dúro sí ojú omi ni.Ó gbìyànjú láti bẹ́ sínú odò náà, ó gbìyànjú láti wọ odò náà, ṣùgbọ́n ó kùnà. Kò lè lọ̀ ìsàlẹ̀ lọ sí oúnjẹ́ náà.
pages.en:
Anansi tried to dive down to the
bottom of the river, but he was a
spider, not a turtle, and he couldn't
dive that deep. He kept floating
back up to the surface again.
He tried jumping in, he tried diving
in, but nothing helped. He just
couldn't get down to that dinner.

pages.text: Lẹ́hin náà Anansi ní àbá kan. Ó kó ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ̀ òkúta sí àpò rẹ̀. Èyí mú kí ó wá wúwo láti lè wọ̀ inú odò.Ó mà gbọ́n gan an ni o!Ó rí tábìlì Ìjàpá, tí ó kún fún àwọn ewé aládùn àtí ọ̀pọ̀lọpọ oúnjẹ dídún. Ẹnu Anansi bẹ̀rẹ̀ sini pòǹgbẹ́ oúnjẹ yìí.
pages.en:
Finally Anansi had an idea. He put
lots of stones in the pockets of his
coat, and finally he was heavy
enough to sink down to the bottom
of the river.
How clever he was!
He saw Turtle's table, full of juicy
green leaves and lots of other
delicious food. Anansi's mouth was
watering.

pages.text:
Bí Anansi ṣe fẹ́ mú lára oúnjẹ yìí, Ìjàpá dadúró. O ní “Anansi, dájúdájú ó kò ní fẹ́ jẹun pẹ̀lú aṣọ rẹ̀? Kì í ṣe bí a ṣe máa ń ṣe nǹkan ní ilé mi.”

Anansi, láí ronú, ní, “Bẹ́ẹ̀ni, òótọ́ lo sọ, Ìjàpá, kí ni mo ń rò?” Ó bọ́ aṣọ rẹ̀.
pages.en:
But just as Anansi was reaching for
some of that delicious food, Turtle
stopped him. "Anansi, surely you're
not going to eat dinner with your
coat on? That's not how we do
things at my house."
Anansi, without thinking, said, "Oh,
of course you're right, Turtle, what
was I thinking?" He took off his
coat.

pages.text:
Ṣùgbọ́n láí sí àwọn òkúta ní àpò rẹ̀ láti mu dúró sí ìsàlẹ̀ odò náà, omi gbé Anansi lọ sí ojú omi padà.

Anansi fi ojú rẹ̀ sínú omi, o sì rí bí Ìjàpá ṣe jẹ gbogbo aládùn náà.
pages.en:
But without the rocks in his pockets
to hold him down, Anansi floated
right back to the surface of the river
again, and popped out of the water.
Anansi sadly put his head down into
the water and watched Turtle eat up
all of the delicious food!

title: Bí imú Ìjàpá ṣe rí kọ́ńbó
author: Taiwo Ẹhinẹni

pages.text:
Ní ìgbà kan, Ìjàpá àti Ọ̀kẹ́rẹ́
jẹ́ ọ̀rẹ́ tímọ́tímọ́. Ní ọjọ́ kan
lẹ́yìn oúnjẹ, Ọ̀kẹ́rẹ́ bi Ìjàpá,
“Ọ̀rẹ́ mi, ọjọ́ ọjà ti fẹ́ dé
ṣùgbọ́n a kò ní owó. Irú iṣẹ́
wo ni a lè ṣe láti pa owó?”
pages.en:
Once upon a time,

Tortoise and Squirrel were very close friends.

One day, Squirrel said to Tortoise, "My friend, we have no money, but market day is getting close.

What business can we do to make some money?"

pages.text:
Ìjàpá dáhùn, “Ṣé o mọ̀ pé mo
máa ń ṣe abọ́. Mo fẹ́ kí o wá
sílé mi kí a jọ̀ ṣe àwọn abọ́
púpọ̀ tí a lè tà.”
“Ó dáa ọ̀rẹ́ mi, a ó pàdé lọ́la
láti ṣe àwọn abọ́ náà,” Ọ̀kẹ́rẹ́
dáhùn.
pages.en: Tortoise responded, "You know I can make clay plates. I want you to join me in making plates to sell." "Okay my friend, tomorrow evening I will join you to make the plates," Squirrel said.

pages.text:
Ní ọjọ́ ọjà, Ìjàpá lọ sí ọjà.
Ó rí àwọn méjì ní ọ̀ọ́kán tí
wón ń jà. Kíá, ó gbé àwọn
abọ́ rẹ̀ sílẹ̀, ó sì lọ síbi ìjà náà.
pages.en:
On the day of the market,

Tortoise went to the marketplace.

He saw two people fighting in the distance. He put down his clay plates and went to watch the fight.

pages.text:
Nígbà tí ó débẹ̀, ó ri pé ọ̀rẹ́
rẹ̀ Ọ̀kẹ́rẹ́ ni ó ń jà pẹ̀lú Ẹmọ́.
pages.en: When Tortoise got there, he saw that it was his friend Squirrel fighting with Mole.

pages.text:
Níkété tí ó débẹ̀, láì wádì oun
tí ó fa ìjà náà, Ìjàpá mú igi ńlá
o sì bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ní í na Ẹmọ́.
“Fi ọ̀rẹ́ mi sílẹ̀!” Ìjàpá kígbe.
pages.en:
Immediately, without finding out what caused the fight,

Tortoise took a big stick and began to beat Mole. "Leave my friend alone!" shouted Tortoise.

pages.text:
Lẹ́hìn náà, Ẹmọ́ dojúkọ Ìjàpá
ó sì bu imú rẹ̀ jẹ.
pages.en:
Mole turned to face

Tortoise and bit him deeply on the nose.

pages.text: Imú Ìjàpá bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ní ṣẹ̀jẹ̀.
pages.en: Tortoise's nose began to bleed.

pages.text:
Ìjàpá ti bẹ́ sínú ìjà Ọ̀kẹ́rẹ́ àti
Ẹmọ́ láìronú.
Láti ọjọ́ yìí ni imú Ìjàpá ti rí
kọ́ńbó tí ó kọ́ wa pé àìfara
balẹ̀ kò dára.
pages.en:
Tortoise had impatiently entered into the fight.

Since that day, Tortoise has a crooked nose to remind him not to be so hasty.

pages.text: Adùn rẹwà púpọ̀. Gbogbo ọkùnrin ní abúlé rẹ̀ ni ó fẹ́ fẹ́ ẹ. Ṣùgbọ́n Adùn kò gbà fún wọn.
pages.en:
Adun was very beautiful. All the
men in her village wanted to
marry her. But Adun refused
them all.

pages.text: Ní ọjọ́ ọjà kan, ọkùnrin kan yá ẹsẹ̀ láti ọwọ́ ọkùnrin kan, ó tún yá apá àti ara lọ́wọ́ ẹlòmíràn. Lẹ́hìn náà, ọkùnrin yìí pa gbogbo ẹ̀yà yìí pọ̀ pẹ̀lú orí rẹ̀. Ó sì lọ sí ọjà.
pages.en:
One market day, a man
borrowed legs from another
man, and arms from another,
and a body from a third man.
Then this man joined all the
parts together. He put his head
on top and went to the market.

pages.text: Ọkùnrin yìí fẹ́ Adùn, ó sì pinu láti fẹ́ ẹ. Adùn náà fẹ́ràn ìmúra ọkùnrin yìí, ó sì fẹ́ wà pẹ̀lú rẹ̀. Ọkùnrin yìí wá láti ìlú jínjìn. Adùn sì pinu láti padà pẹ̀lú rẹ̀.
pages.en:
This man wanted Adun and was
determined to marry her. Adun
was pleased by his appearance.
She wanted to be with him. The
man came from a far town, and
Adun decided to return with
him.

pages.text: Bí Adùn àti ọkùnrin náà ṣe ń lọ́ sí ìlú rẹ̀, ẹni tó ni ẹsẹ̀ gba ẹsẹ̀ náà padà. Lẹ́hìn náà, ẹni tó ni apá gba apá náà padà. Ẹni tó ni ara náà gba ara náà padà.
pages.en:
As Adun and the man journeyed
to his place, the owner of the
legs took the legs back.
Then the owner of the arms
took his arms back.
And finally the owner of the
body took that back.

pages.text: Orí nìkan ni ó kù, orí náà sì ń rìn lọ. Adùn bẹ̀rẹ̀ sì í bẹ̀rù ṣùgbọ́n kò sá lọ. Wọ́n dé ilé orí náà.
pages.en:
Only the head was left, and the
head went on. Adun was scared
but she did not run away. They
arrived at the house of the
head.

pages.text: Ní ọjọ́ kẹjì, kí orí náà tó lọ sí oko rẹ̀, ó sọ fún Ìjàpá, “Tí Adùn bá fẹ́ sá lọ, fọn fèrè yìí láti tó mi létí.”
pages.en:
The following morning, before
the head went to his farm, he
spoke to Tortoise. "If Adun tries
to escape, blow this horn to tell
me," said the head.

pages.text: Bí orí náà ṣe fẹ́ máa lọ, Adùn bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ní í kó ẹrù rẹ̀. Lẹ́hìn náà, ó bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí ní í sá lọ.
pages.en:
After the head left, Adun packed
her things. Then she began to
run away.

pages.text: Nígbà tí Ìjàpá ri, ó fọn fèrè, “Orí, orí, Adùn fẹ́ sá lọ̀” Ìjàpá kígbe.”
pages.en:
Seeing her, Tortoise blew the
horn, "Head, head, Adun is
about to run away," puffed
Tortoise.

pages.text: Orí náà sá lọ bá Adùn. “Ó ní “Níbo ni o rò pé o ń lọ?” Adùn padà lọ sí ilé orí náà.
pages.en:
The head went up to Adun and
said, "Where do you think you
are going?"
Adun went back to the head's
house.

pages.text: Lẹ́hìn náà, Adùn lọ bá babaláwo láti mọ nǹkan tí òun lè ṣe. Babaláwo náà sọ fún, “Lọ ra àwọn àkàrà. Fi àwọn kan sínú epo pupa, kí o sì fi sínú ìho Ìjàpá.”
pages.en:
Eventually Adun consulted a
diviner about what to do. The
diviner advised, "Go and buy
some bean cakes. Soak them in
palm oil and put them in
Tortoise's horn."

pages.text: Adùn tẹ̀lé ìlànà babaláwo náà.
pages.en:
Adun followed the diviner's
instructions. She put the oily
cakes into the horn.

pages.text: Ní ọjọ́ kejì, ó kó àwọn nǹkan rẹ̀, ó sì bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í sá lọ. Nígbà tí Ìjàpá mú ìho láti fọn, àwọn àkàrà aládùn náà bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í jábọ́ sí ẹnu rẹ̀.
pages.en:
The following day, she took her
things and began to run away
again. When Tortoise took the
horn to blow it, the delicious
bean cakes fell into his mouth.

pages.text: Ìjàpá jẹ, jẹ, jẹ. Adùn sì sá lọ.
pages.en:
Tortoise ate, ate and ate.
And Adun ran away.

pages.text: Ní ayé àtijọ́, ní ààfin-ọba kan, ọba kan wà tí ó ní ọmọbìnrin awẹ́lẹ́wà kan.
pages.en:
Once upon a time in a big
palace, there lived a king and
his
beautiful daughter, the
princess.

pages.text: Eerin ń gbé ni ilé kan lẹ́gbẹ̀ẹ́ ààfin. Ọ̀gà ń gbé ní ilé mìíràn ní òdìkejì ààfin.
pages.en:
Elephant lived in a house on
one side of the palace.
Chameleon
lived on the other side.

pages.text: Ní àkókò yìí, ọ̀gbẹlẹ́ kan wà ní gbogbo ilú. Èrò kan sọ sí ọba nínú ó sì pe àwọn aládùúgbò mejèèjì sí ààfin.
pages.en:
At this time, there was a terrible
drought across the land.
The king had an idea and called
his two neighbours to the
palace.

pages.text: Ọba náà wí fún Eerin àti Ọ̀gà pé “ mo fẹ́ kí ẹ máa fi ẹsẹ̀ janlẹ̀ títí omi yòó fi rú jádé.” Ọba ṣe ìlèrí láti fi ọmọbìnrin rẹ̀ fún ẹnikẹ́ni tí ó bá lè ṣe àṣeyọrí.
pages.en:
The kind said to Elephant and
Chameleon, "I want you to
stomp
on the ground with your feet
until water comes out."
The king promised the princess
in marriage to the one who
succeeded.

pages.text: Ọ̀gà kò ní ìrètí nítorí pé ó kéré púpọ̀. Inú Eerin dùn púpọ̀ nítorí pé ó tóbi ó sì ní agbára. Eerin lọ sí orí ilẹ̀, ó sì bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí fi ẹsẹ̀ janlẹ̀.
pages.en:
Chameleon had no hope since
he was very small.
Elephant was extremely happy
since he was so big and
powerful.
Elephant went to the field and
started stomping on the
ground.

pages.text: Eruku bo ilẹ̀, ṣùgbọ́n omi kò jáde. Eerin fi ẹsẹ̀ janlẹ̀ títí omi fi fẹ́ bẹ́rẹ́ sí i sun jáde, ṣùgbọ́n ó ti rẹ̀ ẹ́. Ó fún Ọ̀gà ní àyè láti gbìyànjú.
pages.en:
A lot of dust came, but no
water.
Elephant stomped on the
ground until water was almost
coming out, but he was too
tired.
He gave Chameleon a chance
to try.

pages.text: Ọ̀gà bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí fí ẹsẹ̀ janlẹ̀. Láìpẹ́, omi sun jáde. Ẹnu sì ya àwọn ènìyàn!
pages.en:
Chameleon started stomping on
the ground. After a short while,
water came out.
People could not believe their
eyes!

pages.text: Nítorí náà, ọba fi ọmọbìnrin rẹ̀ fún Ọ̀gà láti fẹ́. Eerin sì lọ si ilé rẹ̀ pẹ̀lú ìbínú.
pages.en:
So the King gave the beautiful
princess to Chameleon.
Elephant went home annoyed.

pages.text: Bóòlù.
pages.en: Ball.

pages.text: Bóòlù mi.
pages.en: My ball.

pages.text: Bóòlù mi tí ó púpa.
pages.en: My red ball.

pages.text: Bóòlù mi tí ó púpa àti tí ó tóbi.
pages.en: My big red ball.

pages.text: Mo ń fi ẹsẹ̀ gbá.
pages.en: I kick.

pages.text: Mo ń fi ẹsẹ̀ gbá bóòlù mi.
pages.en: I kick my ball.

pages.text: Mo ń fi ẹsẹ̀ gbá bóòlù mi tí ó púpa.
pages.en: I kick my red ball.

pages.text: Mo ń fi agbára fi ẹsẹ̀ gbá bóòlù mi tí ó púpa!
pages.en: I kick my red ball hard!

pages.text: Níbo lo wà?
pages.en: Where?

pages.text: Níbo ni bóòlù mi wà?
pages.en: Where is my ball?

pages.text: Níbo ni bóòlù mi wà nísínsinyìí?
pages.en: Where is my ball now?

pages.text: Níbo ni bóòlù mi tí ó púpa wà nísínsinyìí?
pages.en:
Where is my red ball
now?

pages.text: O wà lókè.
pages.en: It is up.

pages.text: O wà lókè lókè.
pages.en: It is high up.

pages.text: O wà lókè ní ọ̀run.
pages.en: It is high up in the sky.

pages.text: Ó wà lókè lókè ní ọ̀run. Ó wà sórí òṣùpá. Ó ti lọ!
pages.en:
It is high up in the sky.
It is over the moon.
It is gone!

title: Ìdí tí wọn kò sin Ajao
author: Taiwo Ẹhinẹni

pages.text: Ajao, àdán kan, sùn sí ilé rẹ̀ nínú àárẹ̀. Kòsí ẹnikẹ́ni tí ó yojú sí i.
pages.en:
Ajao, a bat, lay in his house very ill.

There was no one to attend to him.

pages.text: Lẹ́yìn náà, Ajao kú.
pages.en: Then, Ajao died.

pages.text: Àwọn aládùúgbò ní, "Ajao ti kú, a gbọdọ̀ pe àwọn ẹbí rẹ̀ láti wá sín."
pages.en: The neighbours said, "Ajao is dead. We must call his relations to come and bury him."

pages.text: Àwọn aládùúgbò lọ pe àwọn ẹyẹ pé, "Ìkan lára yín ti kú."
pages.en: The neighbours went and called the birds saying, "A relative of yours is dead."

pages.text: Àwọn ẹyẹ wá, wọ́n sì ri pé Ajao ni. Wọ́n ní, "Ẹranko yìí kì í ṣe ara ẹbí wa."
pages.en:
The birds came and saw that it was Ajao.

They said, "This animal is not part of our family."

pages.text: "Gbogbo ẹbí wa ní ìyẹ́ ṣùgbọ́n Ajao kò ní nǹkankan. Nítorí náà, kì í ṣe ara wa." Àwọn ẹyẹ náà sálọ.
pages.en:
"All our family have feathers but Ajao has none. So, he is not one of us."

The birds went away.

pages.text: Àwọn aládùúgbò ronú papọ̀, wọ́n ní, "Òòtọ́ ni àwọn ẹyẹ sọ. Ajao kò ní ìyẹ́. Nítorí náà, kì í ṣe ara wọn."
pages.en: The neighbours reasoned together. They agreed, "The birds are right. Ajao has no feathers. So, he is not their relative."

pages.text: Ìkan lára wọn ní, "Ó gbọdọ̀ jẹ́ ìkan lára àwọn eku. Ó jọ wọ́n."
pages.en: One of them said, "He must be part of the family of rats. He looks like them."

pages.text: Àwọn aládùúgbò lọ pe àwọn eku pé, "Ìkan lára àwọn ẹbí yín ti kú."
pages.en: The neighbours went and called the rats saying, "One of your family is dead."

pages.text: Àwọn eku wá, wọ́n sì ri pé Ajao ni. Wọ́n ní, "Ẹranko yìí kì í ṣe ara ẹbí wa."
pages.en:
The rats came and saw that it was Ajao.

They said, "This animal is not part of our family."

pages.text: "Gbogbo ẹbí wa ní ìrù ṣùgbọ́n Ajao kò ní ìrù."Àwọn eku náà rìn lọ.
pages.en:
"Everyone in our family has a tail. Ajao has no tail."

The rats went away.

pages.text: A kò rí ẹbí fún Ajao, ó sì wà bẹ́ẹ̀ láì sí ẹni tí yóò sín in.
pages.en: No relations were found for Ajao and he remained unburied.

title: Ọjọ́ tí Òòrùn rin ìrinajò
title_en: The day the sun went away
author: Khothatso Ranoosi, Marion Drew

pages.text: Òòrùn pinnu láti lọ kí àbúrò rẹ̀ obìnrin, òṣùpá. Òṣùpá ń gbé ní òdìkejì òfuurufú.‘Mo máa padà dé láìpẹ́, Òòrùn sọ fún ìkuukù.
pages.en:
Mother Sun decided to visit her sister, the moon.

Sister Moon lives on the other side of the sky. "I will be back soon," said Sun to the clouds.

pages.text: Kò pẹ́ tí Òòrùn jáde lọ, àwọn òkè wé gèlè funfun.
pages.en: When Sun left, the mountains put on their white scarves.

pages.text:
Afẹ́fẹ́ ń ṣàríyànjiyàn pẹ̀lú àwọn igi.

Inú bí àwọn igi.

Wọ́n fọ́n gbogbo ewé wọn ká ibi gbogbo.
pages.en:
Wind had an argument with the trees.

The trees became angry.

They threw their leaves all over the place.

pages.text: Òfuurufú bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí i kùn.Ó yírá padà sí òféèfé.
pages.en:
The sky started to grumble.

She turned grey.

pages.text:
Inú àwọn ìkuukù kò dùn láti rí ohun tí ó ń ṣẹlẹ̀.

Wọ́n bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í sunkún.Ẹkún púpọ̀ wà.
pages.en:
The clouds were sad to see all this.

They started crying.

There were many tears.

pages.text: Gbogbo àgbáyé bẹ̀rẹ̀ sí í rì wọnú omi lọ.
pages.en: The whole world began to sink under water.

pages.text:
Bẹ́ẹ̀ kẹ̀dẹ̀ ré, ní apá kejì òfuurufú, Òòrùn ti ṣetán láti kúrò lọ́dọ̀ àbúrò rẹ̀.

Wọ́n fẹnu konu, ó kí òṣùpá pé ó dìgbà ó sì padà sí ilé.
pages.en:
Meanwhile, on the other side of the sky,

Sun was ready to leave her sister.

She kissed the moon goodbye and went home.

pages.text: Inú òfuurufù dùn púpọ̀ láti rí Òòrùn tó bẹ́ẹ̀ tí ó sì yípadà sí àwọ̀ búlù.Àwọn òkè wọ àsọ aláwọ̀-ewé wọn.
pages.en:
Sky was so happy to see Sun that she turned bright blue.

The mountains put on their pretty green dresses.

pages.text:
Afẹ́fẹ́ lọ sùn.

Awọn igi na ẹ̀ka wọn, wọ́n sì rẹ́rìn-ín.
pages.en:
The wind went to sleep.

The trees stretched their branches and smiled.

pages.text:
Inú àwọn ìkuukù dùn láti rí Òòrùn padà.

Wọ́n jádé lọ ṣeré.
pages.en:
The clouds were very happy to see mother Sun again.

They went away to play.

pages.text:
Ọ̀pọ̀ àwọn ewéko kéèkèèké hù jáde láti inú ilẹ̀ láti ṣe “ báwo ni?”

Gbogbo àgbáyé ń tàn yinrin.
pages.en:
Lots of little plants popped out of the earth to say, "Hello."

The whole world sparkled.

pages.text:
Òòrún tan ìtànṣán rẹ̀ sí ibi gbogbo.

Pẹ̀lú ayọ̀, ó ní “Mo wí fún yín pé n óò padà wá.”
pages.en: Mother Sun shone her light everywhere."I told you I would be back," she beamed.

pages.text:
Padà wá, olóńgbò!
Ṣeré pẹ̀lú mi.
pages.en: Come back, cat! Play with me.

pages.text:
Jòkó sínú apẹ̀rẹ̀ rẹ.
Dúró síbí!
pages.en:
Sit in your basket. Stay
right here!

pages.text:
Padà wá, olóńgbò!
Ọ̀nà yẹn ti ga jù.
pages.en: Come back, cat! That's way too high.

pages.text:
Padà wá, olóńgbò!
Má lọ síta.
pages.en: Come back, cat! Don't go outside.

pages.text:
Padà wá, olóńgbò!
Iyẹn kì í ṣe tìrẹ.
pages.en: Come back, cat! That's not yours.

pages.text:
Padà wá, olóńgbò!
Kí ni o ní?
pages.en: Come back, cat! What have you got?

pages.text:
Padà wá, olóńgbò!
Iyẹn kì í ṣe ọ̀rẹ́ rẹ.
pages.en: Come back, cat! That's not your friend!

pages.text:
Báwo ni, olóńgbò!
Ṣé o ti padà?
pages.en: Hello, cat! Are you back?

pages.text:
Dúró sínú apẹ̀rẹ̀ rẹ.
Àkókò oorun ti yá.
pages.en: Stay in your basket. It's nap time now.

pages.text: Olóńgbò?
pages.en: Cat?

pages.text: Gbogbo ènìyàn mọ̀ pé eerin ní imú gígùn.
Ṣùgbọ́n ní àyé àtijọ́, imú eerìn kúrú ó sì tóbi.

Lẹ́yìn tí wọ́n bí ọmọ eerin kan. Ó bẹ púpọ̀.

Kò sí ẹranko tí kò ní ìbéèrè fún.
Ó fẹ́ mọ́ nípa àgùnfọn.Ó bèrè lọ́wọ́ àgùnfọn “Kí ló dé tí o ní ọrùn gígùn?"
Bákan náà ní ó bèrè lọ́wọ́ Túrùkí."Kí lo dé tí ó ni ìhò tí ó ní orí ṣóńṣó?"
Ó tún fẹ́ mọ̀ nípa Ọ̀ọ̀nì náà.Ó bèèrè lọ́wọ́ rẹ̀, “Kí ni àwọn ọ̀ọ̀nì máa ń jẹ fún oúnjẹ alẹ́?”
Ẹyẹ Àgbìgbò ọlọ́gbọ́n kan dáa lóhùn,“Tẹ̀lé mi lọ sí odò, níbẹ̀ ni ìwọ yóò ti rí ohun tí ọ̀ọ̀nì ń jẹ fún oúnjẹ alẹ́.”
Ọmọ Eerin tẹ̀lé àgbìgbò lọ sí odò.
Ó rìn kọjá láàárín àwọn koríkò etí odò láti lè dúró létí odò.Ó wo inú odò.“Níbo ni Ọ̀ọ̀ni wà?”

Òkùta kan tí ó wà lẹ́gbẹ̀ẹ́ odò náà kí i pé “báwo ni?”Ọmọ Eerin náà dáhùn pé “dáádá ni.”

O ní “ ṣe o lè sọ fún mi ohun tí Ọ̀ọ̀nì mán ń jẹ fún oúnjẹ alẹ́?”

Òkùta náà dáhùn pé “ súnmọ́ ibí yìí, n óò sọ ọ́ fún ẹ.” Ọmọ Eerin dorí kodò.

Okùta ní “Súnmọ́ ibí dáadáa.”Ọmọ Eerin túbọ̀ dorí kodò.
Lójijì ! À fi pàkà!Ọ̀ọ̀ni di eyín mọ́ imú ọmọ Eerin.

Kò pẹ́, ọmọ Eerin ṣubú.“kòròbàtà!!”
Imú ọmọ Eerin tí ó kúrú tẹ́lẹ̀ tí gùn jádé.

Imú rẹ̀ gùn gan-an ni, kódà ó lè fi imú rẹ̀ já èèso láti ara ẹ̀ka-igi tí ó ga fíofío.

Títí di òní, Eerin ní imú ti ó gùn tí ó sì wúlò fún un.
